public_rationale: Microsoft demonstrated Bing on February 7, 2023, and Google held its Paris presentation on February 8 [e1, e3]. Microsoft described a limited preview using an OpenAI language model; Google's February 6 announcement described Bard as an experimental LaMDA service opening to trusted testers [e1, e2]. These records support the comparison of language-model tools with restricted access and unresolved reliability problems [e1, e2, e4]. AP's February 8 report documented Bard's false telescope answer and Bing's invented result for a Super Bowl that had yet to occur [e4]. Bard's error appeared in its earlier advertisement [e3]. Ars Technica sharply criticized Google's Paris presentation, while a February 9 roundup reported praise for Bing as a major change in accessing information [e3, e6]. These examples support the reception contrast within February 6–9, although AP also criticized Bing and a favorable attendee review credited its integration [e3, e4, e5, e6].
limitations: The coverage examples do not establish how common either reaction was or show unanimous reception [e3–e6].
Restricted access and documented errors do not provide an objective test of public readiness or establish equal accuracy [e1, e2, e4].
The event records establish adjacent calendar dates, without establishing a strict 24-hour interval [e1, e3].
The February 9 roundup supports reception within the target period; it does not establish that this roundup was available before Marcus published [e6].

conditions: neither fully ready for public use

statement.excerpt: The two megacompanies both demoed prototypes, neither fully ready for public use, built around apparently comparable technology, facing apparently similar bugs, within a day of each other. Yet one demo was presented as a revolution, the other as a disaster.
statement.document_title: Oops! How Google bombed, while doing pretty much exactly the same thing as Microsoft did, with similar results

from_speaker: neither fully ready for public use
within a day of each other
one demo was presented as a revolution, the other as a disaster
our_interpretation: The target is the launch-week demonstrations and reception discussed in the February 9 post, covering February 6–9, 2023.

Within a day means demonstrations on adjacent calendar dates: Microsoft's February 7 event and Google's February 8 Paris event. Google's February 6 Bard announcement is distinguished from its Paris presentation.
Prototypes and not fully ready mean experimental or preview systems with restricted access and unresolved reliability problems. This does not mean nobody could use them.
Apparently comparable technology means language-model-based conversational information tools, without requiring identical models, integrations, capabilities, or accuracy.
Apparently similar bugs means factual errors presented as answers, without requiring equal error rates.
The reception contrast means prominent contemporary examples of transformative praise for Bing and sharply negative treatment of Google. It does not require unanimous coverage or those exact labels.
criteria.support_condition: Records establish adjacent-day demonstrations, experimental or preview status, broadly comparable language-model technology and factual-error problems, together with prominent contemporary examples of the stated reception contrast.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable records materially refute the timing, developmental status, broad technological or error similarity, or claimed reception contrast. Differences in implementation alone do not refute apparent comparability.

evidence.locator: Yusuf Mehdi's closing announcement; transcript header and technical-breakthrough discussion
evidence.explanation: The dated transcript records Microsoft's demonstration, restricted preview and use of a next-generation OpenAI language model. These support the timing, broad technology comparison and unfinished rollout described in the claim.

Google describes a language-model-based experimental service and says access is opening to trusted testers before wider public availability. Its testing plans support the ordinary reading of incomplete public readiness.

evidence.locator: Subtitle; opening paragraphs and Bard discussion
evidence.explanation: This contemporary report supplies the Paris event date and strongly negative reception. It distinguishes Bard's earlier advertisement error from the presentation and reports that Bard remained restricted to testing.

evidence.publisher: Associated Press, syndicated by Tech Xplore
evidence.explanation: AP documents Bard's telescope error and its own test in which Bing invented a completed Super Bowl before the game occurred. This supports similar factual-error problems while showing that contemporary coverage also criticized Bing.

An attendee explicitly favors Microsoft's demonstration over Google's initial Bard showing. His account identifies integration and user experience as reasons, so the reception difference need not imply that the underlying models differed greatly.

evidence.excerpt: Roose isn't alone in his praise.
evidence.locator: Second paragraph; surrounding summaries of New York Times, Wall Street Journal and Inverse reviews
evidence.explanation: The article documents reviewers presenting Bing as a major change in accessing information, supporting the ordinary meaning of revolutionary reception. This is secondary evidence because the New York Times page could not be read directly.
